idiom_name: instance-variable composition with an explicit close and block form
implementation_notes: A Ruby whole is an object whose instance variables are its parts; private/protected methods plus deliberately narrow readers keep the parts away from clients, and no runtime mechanism enforces ownership - the convention lives in the API: a factory returns the whole, the whole creates its parts, and nobody else receives them. Release is explicit: the whole defines close/dispose and the idiomatic block form (Document.open(path) { |doc| ... }) runs that close from an ensure clause even when the block raises, cascading to the parts it owns. ObjectSpace.define_finalizer exists, but the core documentation is blunt that finalization is unpredictable and never guaranteed to be run except on exit, and a finalizer that references the object prevents it from being collected at all - so it is a backstop, never a cleanup path.
pitfalls: dup/clone copy the instance-variable references, so both copies 'own' the same parts and closing both double-closes resources - define initialize_copy or make the whole non-copyable.

ObjectSpace.define_finalizer is documented as unpredictable and never guaranteed except at exit, and a finalizer capturing the object prevents collection altogether; do not put resource release there.
attr_accessor, Struct or OpenStruct exposure of the part collection lets callers push and replace parts behind the whole and break its invariants.
